clinicalPearls: Type I is the only 'primary' 3-methylglutaconic aciduria — a genuine inborn error of leucine catabolism caused by deficiency of 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase (AUH gene); all other numbered types are 'secondary' 3-MGA-urias reflecting disturbed mitochondrial membrane and energy function.

The biochemical hallmark distinguishing type I is marked elevation of both 3-methylglutaconic acid and 3-methylglutaric acid together with raised 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid — a pattern not seen in the secondary forms, where 3-methylglutaconic acid is usually only mildly raised in isolation.

The clinical spectrum is strikingly broad and age-dependent, ranging from children detected incidentally, through infantile developmental and speech delay, to an adult-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy with spasticity, ataxia, dysarthria and cognitive decline.
Unlike type II (Barth syndrome) it does not cause cardiomyopathy or neutropenia, and unlike type III (Costeff syndrome) it is not primarily an optic atrophy syndrome.
Quantitative urine organic acid analysis is the key screening test; deficient enzyme activity in fibroblasts or biallelic AUH variants confirm the diagnosis.
A leucine-restricted diet and carnitine supplementation have been tried, but a disease-modifying benefit remains unproven and care is largely supportive.
Adult presentations may mimic acquired leukoencephalopathy or a slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder, so organic acids should be considered in unexplained white-matter disease.
reference.pathophysiology: 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria type I is an autosomal recessive inborn error caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in AUH, which encodes 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase, a mitochondrial enzyme catalysing the fifth step of leucine degradation, the hydration of 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA to 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA); the protein is bifunctional, also acting as an RNA-binding protein for AU-rich elements. Enzyme deficiency blocks the leucine catabolic pathway, so 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA accumulates and is hydrolysed to 3-methylglutaconic and 3-methylglutaric acids, while upstream metabolism yields raised 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid. This authentic pathway block distinguishes type I from the secondary 3-MGA-urias, in which 3-methylglutaconic acid appears as an indirect marker of impaired inner-membrane phospholipid remodelling and oxidative phosphorylation rather than a direct enzyme defect.
additionalDifferentials: 3-MGA type II (Barth syndrome, TAZ/tafazzin) — X-linked, with cardiomyopathy, neutropenia and skeletal myopathy
3-MGA type III (Costeff optic atrophy syndrome, OPA3) — early optic atrophy with later extrapyramidal signs
MEGDEL syndrome (SERAC1) — 3-MGA with sensorineural deafness and a Leigh-like encephalopathy
Other adult leukoencephalopathies and slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorders
Other organic acidurias raising 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid (HMG-CoA lyase deficiency, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency)
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urine organic acids showing 3-methylglutaconic, 3-methylglutaric and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acids
AUH gene sequencing or targeted metabolic gene panel
3-Methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase enzyme activity assay in cultured fibroblasts
Brain MRI to assess white-matter signal change in symptomatic and adult cases
Echocardiography and full blood count to exclude type II (Barth)
Ophthalmological assessment to exclude type III (Costeff)
redFlags: Progressive spasticity, ataxia or cognitive decline in a young adult with unexplained leukoencephalopathy
Acute metabolic decompensation with acidosis during intercurrent illness in infancy
Emergence of cardiomyopathy or neutropenia, which should redirect towards type II (Barth)
reference.prognosis: The course is highly variable: many individuals remain mildly affected or stable, while others develop a slowly progressive adult leukoencephalopathy with motor and cognitive decline. No proven disease-modifying therapy exists.
pitfalls: Assuming that any 3-methylglutaconic aciduria equals type I — most are secondary, and only type I shows the full leucine-pathway metabolite pattern with raised 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid.
Overlooking the diagnosis in adults who present as neurodegeneration or leukoencephalopathy rather than a childhood metabolic illness.
Relying on a single urine sample, as metabolite excretion can fluctuate.
Attributing cardiac or haematological features to type I, as these instead point to type II (Barth).
